name: Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg
hover_description: Würzburg, 1626–1631: ~300 executions including 19 Catholic priests and the prince-bishop's nephew. One of the most intensive German superhunts.
panel_description:
The Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg experienced approximately 300 executions between 1626 and 1631, running almost simultaneously with the parallel Bamberg prosecution sixty-five kilometers to the north and sharing with it the structural features that Midelfort identifies as the defining pattern of the German Catholic 'superhunt': prosecution conducted by a Prince-Bishop who combined ecclesiastical and secular authority in a territory without effective external oversight, during the Thirty Years' War period's compounding of confessional anxiety and social disruption. The Würzburg prosecution was notable above all for the social breadth of its victims: among those executed were the Prince-Bishop's nephew, members of the cathedral chapter, the court physician, the town clerk, students, and children. Nineteen Catholic priests were executed — a figure that demonstrates the cascade mechanism's capacity to dissolve any institutional barrier once fully established.

  Midelfort's Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany (1972) analyzes Würzburg alongside Bamberg as a paired example of the Catholic Prince-Bishopric superhunt pattern — the two territories that together demonstrate most clearly how the combination of unchecked prosecutorial authority, the torture-confession-denunciation cascade, and the theoretical framework of diabolical conspiracy could produce mass killing across an entire society. The prosecution of clergy and the Prince-Bishop's own family members at Würzburg illustrates Midelfort's key analytical point about the superhunt's self-defeating character: once the cascade reached elite and well-connected victims, it either terminated through resistance or began to consume the very institutional elites who had authorized it.

  Friedrich Spee's Cautio Criminalis (1631), the most important contemporary critique of witch prosecution procedure, was written while Spee was serving as confessor to those condemned in the Würzburg trials. Spee did not himself name Würzburg in the text — the Cautio was published anonymously, and his authorship was not publicly identified in his lifetime — but the confessors' experience of men and women begging for absolution who Spee was convinced were innocent directly motivated his systematic critique of the torture procedure that sustained prosecution. Würzburg is therefore simultaneously one of the most intensive execution sites and the indirect cause of the most consequential internal Catholic critique of the witch hunt.
administrative_context: Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg was an ecclesiastical territorial state in Franconia, Holy Roman Empire. Like Bamberg (its neighbor, 65km north), it combined episcopal and secular authority under a Prince-Bishop who could deploy both canonical and secular criminal law against accused witches.
witchcraft_trials_significance: The Würzburg witch hunt of 1626–1631 ran simultaneously with the Bamberg hunt and was similarly catastrophic. Approximately 300 people were executed, including 19 Catholic priests, the prince-bishop's own nephew, and multiple court officials. The prosecution's reach through all social strata — including clergy — made Würzburg particularly shocking to contemporaries and to subsequent historians. The Hunt was ended by the Swedish invasion during the Thirty Years War, not by any internal check.

key_magistrates.name: Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg
key_magistrates.contribution_to_trials: Authorized and sustained the prosecution; was himself reportedly accused in confessions (not prosecuted) by the end of the hunt

persecution_timeline.1626: Initial executions following crop failures and the same regional panic that triggered Bamberg
persecution_timeline.1629: Peak: 19 executions in December 1629 including several priests
persecution_timeline.1630–1631: Continuation until Swedish occupation ends the prosecution

affected_population.geographic_extent: Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg and surrounding Franconian territories
affected_population.social_reach: All strata; notably included 19 Catholic priests and multiple civic officials

scholarly_analysis.clark_perspective: Würzburg demonstrates that the superhunt dynamic was not constrained by clerical status — even ordained priests were among the executed, showing that the denunciation spiral recognized no institutional boundary.
scholarly_analysis.hutton_perspective: The prosecution of clergy at Würzburg is Hutton's primary example of the social-ceiling effect of denunciation cascades: when high-status individuals begin to be accused, the hunt either terminates through resistance or consumes the elites generating the accusations.
scholarly_analysis.ginzburg_perspective: Würzburg's scope confirms the Ginzburg argument about the self-fulfilling character of the confession dynamic — the apparent conspiracy grew in direct proportion to prosecution intensity.

legacy_and_historiographical_importance: Friedrich Spee served as confessor to condemned witches at Würzburg (as well as Trier) and his experiences at both sites directly motivated the Cautio Criminalis (1631). Würzburg is therefore a double contribution to witch-trial historiography: as one of the most intensive prosecution sites and as the experience that produced the most important contemporary critique of prosecution procedure.
primary_sources: Trial records in Würzburg episcopal archives; contemporary accounts cited in Behringer; Friedrich Spee's Cautio Criminalis (1631) composed partly in response to Würzburg experiences
source_method: Brian Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (3rd ed., 2006); Wolfgang Behringer, Witches and Witch-Hunts (2004); Stuart Clark, Thinking with Demons (1997/2001)
